questions.question: Discuss how the concepts of isostasy help to explain the post-glacial rebound of different regions on Earth. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Isostasy refers to the gravitational equilibrium between the Earth’s lithosphere and the
  • Asthenosphere. -1 mark
  • Post-glacial rebound or Glacial isostatic adjustment is a natural response of the Earth’s
  • crust to be uplifted as a result of the retreat of large ice sheets/glaciers. -1 mark
  • The lithosphere is assumed to float over the layer of asthenosphere, which is of a plastic
  • nature.
  • Two classical models that describe isostasy are
  • Airy’s model – variations in crustal thickness compensate for topographic differences.
  • Pratt’s model – variations in crustal density compensate for elevation differences
  • -2 marks
  • The additional weight of huge ice sheets causes the lithosphere to sink deep into
  • Asthenosphere.
  • When the weight of the ice sheets is removed as the ice melts down by climatic change
  • of interglacial periods, the lithosphere rises or rebounds to regain equilibrium by the
  • redistri-bution of mantle material and asthenosphere.
  • Recent satellite data show measurable uplift in Antarctica and Greenland ice sheets thin
  • due to climate change -2 marks

  • Built by fluid basaltic lava flowing easily ov er large areas. Slopes are gentle (6º –12º) from

  • Hawaii and Iceland. Composition (3 marks)- Formed from basaltic (mafic) magma with ~50%
  • silica, low viscosity, and high magnesium and iron content. Produces dark -colored basalt
  • rock- Basaltic lava flo ws easily and erupts gently from fissures.Style of Eruption (1 mark) -
  • Gentle, non -explosive eruptions; lava flows move slowly, causing limited damage and
  • allowing evacuation.

questions.question: Discuss the differences between tectonic and volcanic earthquakes. Describe their causes, typical locations, and key characteristics. / [CO5] [8x6 = 48]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the differences between tectonic and volcanic earthquakes. Describe t heir
  • causes, typical locations, and key characteristics.
  • Definition & Main Distinction (1 mark) - Tectonic earthquakes: Caused by brittle rupture/slip
  • along faults from accumulated elastic stress due to plate motion.Volcanic (magmatic)
  • earthquakes: Caused by movement or pressure of magma/gas beneath the surface.2.
  • Magnitude & Intensity (1 mark) - Tectonic: Produce the world’s strongest
  • earthquakes.Volcanic: Generally smaller, often occur in swarms before eruptions.3. Typical
  • Locations (1 mark) -Tectonic: Found mainly along plate boundaries (convergent, divergent,
  • transform).-Volcanic: Occur in volcanic regions—hot spots, subduction zones, and spreading
  • centers.4. Causes & Mechanism – Tectonic Earthquakes (2 marks .-Continuous plate
  • movement builds stress along locked faults.When stress > friction, rocks fracture and slip,
  • releasing energy as seismic waves (elastic rebound).Common atConvergent zones (Benioff
  • zone) – strong quakes.Transform faults – horizontal slip (e.g., San Andreas).Divergent
  • ridges – shallow, small quakes.5. Causes & Mechanism – Volcanic Earthquakes (2 marks)-
  • Generated by magma movement and pressure changes within the crust.Often precede
  • volcanic eruptions (earthquake swarms signal magma ascent).Common at subduction
  • zones, hot spots, and diverge nt boundaries.6. Summary/Conclusion (1 mark) - Tectonic
  • earthquakes result from mechanical stress and fault rupture, while . Volcanic earthquakes
  • signal magma movement within or near volcanoes.Both reflect the Earth’s dynamic internal
  • processes.

questions.question: Explain the concept of plate tectonics, and discuss the landforms associated with various plate margins / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the concept of plate tectonics, and discuss the landforms associated with various
  • plate margins.
  • Concept of Plate Tectonics (4 marks) -The theory of plate tectonics explai ns Earth’s
  • dynamic activities — earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building, and continental drift.The
  • lithosphere (crust + upper mantle, ~75 –125 km thick) is broken into tectonic plates. These
  • plates float on the asthenosphere, a weak, partially molten laye r (~350 km deep).Plates
  • move slowly (1 –16 cm/year), and their interactions at boundaries cause most major
  • geological events.( 1 mark for definition, 1 for structure/layers, 1 for movement, 1 for
  • significance).
  • Plate Boundaries and Landforms – 8 marks
  • A. Divergent Boundaries (Spreading Centers) – 3 marks Plates move apart, magma rises to
  • form new lithosphere. Ocean–Ocean: Mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys; sea -floor spreading,
  • shallow earthquakes, volcanoes.Continent –Continent: Rift valleys (e.g., East Afr ican Rift),
  • earthquakes, rising magma, volcanic activity.(marks: 1 for process, 1 for oceanic example, 1
  • for continental example)
  • B. Convergent Boundaries – 3 marks, Plates move toward each other; one may subduct
  • beneath the other, forming trenches and mou ntains.Ocean–Ocean: Island arcs and
  • trenches; subduction, deep earthquakes, volcanoes.Ocean –Continent: Coastal mountains
  • (e.g., Andes); subduction, volcanoes, deformation. Continent –Continent: Collision forms
  • large mountain ranges (e.g., Himalayas), crusta l thickening, folding, thrust faulting(marks
  • Division: 1 for process, 1 for subduction examples, 1 for continental collision)
  • C. Transform Boundaries – 2 marks-Plates slide horizontally past one another along strike -
  • slip faults. Ocean–Ocean: Offset mid-ocean ridges, earthquakes.Continent–Continent: Fault
  • zones (e.g., San Andreas Fault); earthquakes, deformation, uplift.(marks division: 1 for
  • process, 1 for examples/effects)
